opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think a real-time human confirmation loop is very hard to make work as a core safety mechanism for driving, and that's been a fairly consistent view at Waymo for a long time.

The problem is the timescale. Many of the situations that matter on the road unfold in a second or two: a pedestrian steps out, a car runs a light, someone cuts across your lane. If the system has to stop and ask a remote person, "Should I brake here?", you've introduced latency, a dependency on connectivity, and a human who has to build situational awareness from a cold start in a fraction of a second. That's exactly the regime where people perform poorly. We saw this early on with the idea of a human supervising the system and taking over when needed. People become complacent very quickly when the system is good most of the time, and then they're not ready in the moment it counts.

So our philosophy has been that the vehicle itself has to be fully responsible for the safety-critical, real-time driving task. It needs to perceive, predict what other agents will do, and plan a safe response entirely on board, without waiting for anyone.

That doesn't mean humans have no role. There's an important place for what we call remote assistance, but it's a different kind of interaction. If the car encounters something genuinely ambiguous that isn't time-critical, like a road closure with confusing signage, a construction worker waving it through in an unusual way, or a blocked lane where it's unclear whether to go around, the car can stop in a safe state and ask for context. A human can say, "That lane is closed, take this path," and the car still decides how to execute that safely. The human provides high-level guidance, not joystick control and not split-second confirmation.

That design also forces a good discipline on the research side. It means you can't paper over weaknesses in the model by assuming a person will catch them. You have to build systems that are robust to the long tail, that know when they're uncertain, and that can fall back to safe behavior on their own. And the remote assistance interactions become a valuable signal. They show you where the system is still unsure, which feeds back into data mining, simulation, and training so that over time the car needs to ask less and less.

So in short, a real-time human in the loop as a safety backstop for driving decisions doesn't really scale and isn't reliable. Humans as occasional advisors for non-urgent, ambiguous situations, on the other hand, are quite useful, as long as the vehicle remains in charge of keeping everyone safe.

r001.rationale: The response says the vehicle must handle safety-critical driving itself, recognize uncertainty, and fall back to safe behavior without waiting for a person. For ambiguous, non-urgent situations, it says the car can stop safely before asking for guidance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question that comes up a lot, and I think it's worth being precise about what we mean by it. At Waymo, we have what we call fleet response, and I think people sometimes imagine it as a person sitting with a steering wheel remotely driving the car. That is explicitly not what we do, and I think it would be a mistake to build a system that way.

The reason is latency and safety. If you have a real-time loop where a human has to confirm an action before the car takes it, you've now made your safety-critical path dependent on a network connection and on human reaction time, and neither of those is reliable enough for a split-second decision. The car has to be the one responsible for driving safely at all times. It has to be able to handle the immediate situation, come to a safe state on its own, and never be in a position where it's waiting on a human to avoid an accident.

So where humans do come in is at a different timescale and a different level of abstraction. The vehicle encounters something genuinely ambiguous, say a construction zone with unusual cone placement, or a police officer waving traffic through in a way that conflicts with the signal. The car recognizes that it's uncertain, it does the safe thing, which is often to slow down or stop, and then it can ask for guidance. And the guidance is not "turn the wheel left," it's more like "yes, it's okay to proceed through that lane" or "treat this as a closed road." The human is providing context or a higher-level intent, and the car still executes it with all of its own safety checks in place.

I actually think of this as a pretty principled division of labor. Machines are very good at the fast, high-precision, always-attentive part of the problem. Humans are good at the long-tail semantic reasoning, the "what is actually going on in this scene" question, which is exactly where the models still have gaps. And importantly, every one of those interactions becomes data. When the car asks and a human answers, that's a labeled example of a situation the system found hard, and over time we want those to become rarer because the model has learned to handle them.

The other thing I'd say is that the rate matters a lot for the economics and for whether the approach scales. If the car needed confirmation every few minutes, you haven't really built an autonomous system, you've built a very expensive remote-operated one. So we track how often these interventions happen very closely, and the goal is always to push it down. It should be a rare event, not part of the normal driving loop.

r001.rationale: The response says the car must handle immediate situations and reach a safe state on its own; when it recognizes uncertainty, it slows down or stops before requesting human guidance.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between getting help from a human and relying on a human to make a real-time driving decision. If something happens suddenly—a pedestrian steps into the road, for example—the vehicle has to respond on its own. You can’t depend on a network connection or on someone remotely understanding the situation quickly enough.

Where human assistance can be useful is when the vehicle encounters an ambiguous situation and has time to ask for guidance. Perhaps there’s construction and it’s unclear where to proceed. The vehicle can stop safely, request assistance, and use that input to inform its next action. But it still needs to be responsible for executing that action safely. So I see a role for human guidance, but the immediate safety decisions have to stay with the autonomous system.

r001.rationale: The response says the vehicle must handle sudden safety decisions itself and may stop before requesting guidance in an ambiguous situation. It does not clearly state that the vehicle itself must recognize when stopping is required rather than rely on human confirmation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is whether the human is providing assistance or is actually part of the real-time driving loop. If the vehicle encounters an unusual situation, it can be useful to ask a person for some high-level guidance. But you don’t want safety to depend on that person responding immediately. There can be communication delays, the connection can drop, and the person needs time to understand the situation.

So the vehicle has to be able to maintain a safe state on its own while it waits. The human might help clarify how to proceed, but the system still needs to determine whether that action is safe and execute it autonomously. I see that kind of assistance as useful; I’m much less comfortable with an architecture that requires a human confirmation within a tight deadline to avoid a dangerous situation.

r001.rationale: The response says the vehicle must maintain a safe state without relying on an immediate human reply, but it does not state that the vehicle itself must recognize when it needs to stop.
